title: Coordinated action on clean air and climate change can net $15 for every dollar spent
text: A UN-backed report says integrated action on air pollution and climate policy can cut emissions, improve health, and generate strong economic returns.

title: El Niño is surging. Months of extreme heat could follow
text: UN News reports that El Niño is intensifying, with unusually hot conditions likely across many regions in the coming months.

title: Farmers Are Going Broke Amid Rising Gas Prices, While the Ag Secretary Profits Off Them
text: As diesel and fertilizer costs rise and USDA support for cheaper renewables is cut, the report questions the agriculture secretary’s conflict of interest with fossil fuel holdings.

title: The U.S. Wants the Oil From These 17 Venezuelan Fields
text: The report says a private oil company has struck a deal with the Trump administration to develop 17 oil areas in Venezuela.

title: The Winners and Losers of Maine’s Race to Armor Its Shoreline Against Climate Change
text: Maine is racing to harden its shoreline, but communities are not sharing equally in access to protection or the costs of disruption.

title: Analysis: UK solar power hits record high over summer 2026
text: Carbon Brief finds UK solar generation hit a summer record, driven by sunny conditions and continued deployment growth.

title: How this summer’s heat and drought impacted crops in Europe – in six charts
text: Carbon Brief uses six charts to show how this summer’s heat, drought, and wildfires affected European crops.

title: The state of the EU’s climate agenda: into autumn 2026 and beyond
text: E3G argues the EU climate agenda is entering an autumn political window, with energy, security, and extreme-weather pressures reshaping priorities.

title: Analysis: UK solar power hits record high over summer 2026
text:
UK solar generation set a summer record under extreme heat and long daylight, showing that renewable deployment is beginning to turn climate stress into supply gains; the policy implication is that grid dispatch, storage, and interconnection rules must advance in parallel so weather-driven gains become system resilience rather than a short-lived output spike.

The piece responds to the 2026 summer when record heat, unusual sunshine, and record output coincided, showing that ‘more solar’ is no longer just an installation story but a governance problem of system adaptation to extremes. It shifts the debate from capacity growth to system integration.

It sits at the intersection of UK power-market reform and net-zero implementation, directly affecting the policy sequencing of interconnection, storage, and demand-side response.

title: How this summer’s heat and drought impacted crops in Europe – in six charts
text:
European agriculture is not facing a single weather shock but a compound risk in which heat, drought, and wildfires interact with energy prices, fertilizer supply, and fuel costs; the article’s mechanism is that output volatility has become an institutional vulnerability shaped by supply chains, input prices, and adaptation policy, requiring crop insurance, irrigation investment, fertilizer substitution, and food-price buffers to be governed together.

The article lands as governments begin assessing harvest losses, food-price pressure, and farm relief after the summer extremes. It moves short-term crop failures into Europe’s medium-term food-security and adaptation-finance agenda.

It sits at the intersection of EU agriculture and food-security policy, adaptation strategy, and the next round of loss-and-damage debates.

title: The state of the EU’s climate agenda: into autumn 2026 and beyond
text:
E3G places the EU climate agenda within a politics of independence and vulnerability, arguing that trade, technology, security, and extreme weather are pushing climate policy beyond a narrow emissions frame toward strategic resilience; the implication is that without aligning industrial policy, energy security, and climate goals, the EU will struggle to sustain coherence and implementation through the autumn window.

The commentary directly targets the EU’s autumn legislative and coordination period, responding to the way security and industrial pressures have crowded the climate agenda. Its timing is political rather than data-driven: the hierarchy of priorities has already shifted.

It sits at the intersection of the Commission’s ‘independence moment’ narrative, member-state priority competition, and the next phase of climate implementation.

title: Gatekeeping the Greenland ice sheet: climate change data and the “upstream” production of global governance objects
source: Lin Alexandra Mortensgaard · European Journal of International Relations
text:
The article develops ‘gatekeeping’ to show that global governance objects are shaped not at the point of published results, but upstream when data are scoped, extracted, and preliminarily analyzed. Through multi-sited ethnography of Greenland ice-core science, the author shows how states and scientific institutions control the flow and content of raw climate data and moves data sovereignty to the start of knowledge production.

The author uses multi-sited ethnography, combining participant observation and semi-structured interviews across Greenland, Germany, and Denmark, to trace ice-core science in practice.

Read alongside this issue’s Carbon Brief piece on UK solar’s record output: both show that energy and climate governance are shaped not only at the results stage, but by how data, infrastructure, and institutional thresholds are set upstream.

Who controls raw climate data in governance settings? data sovereignty climate science gatekeeping ethnography How does upstream knowledge production shape policy outcomes? knowledge production global governance institutional power climate data

title: Melting Himalayas
text: Flooding and glacier risk in the Nepal–Tibet region put Himalayan hazard cascades front and center, showing how cryosphere change is reshaping downstream exposure.

title: Trump Says U.S. Struck Deal for Control of More Than 65 Billion Barrels of Venezuela’s Oil
text: Trump said the United States had reached a deal over control of Venezuela’s oil, with the arrangement reportedly channelled through a private company.

title: The Nepal floods seem a world away – but make no mistake, climate breakdown will affect us all | Nesrine Malik
text: Placing Nepal’s floods beside Europe’s heatwaves, the piece argues climate loss is not a distant event but a shared risk magnified by unequal fiscal and adaptive capacity.

title: Texas and Louisiana could get hit by a fast-spin-up tropical storm on Tuesday
text: A small system over very warm offshore waters could intensify quickly, creating sudden storm risk for Texas and Louisiana.

title: Why Iceland Chose Fish Over European Alliances
text: Iceland’s vote to reject reopening EU accession talks shows fisheries interests again outweigh deeper European integration.

title: Will a Data Center Join the Philadelphia Bellwether District’s Mix of Manufacturers and Warehouses?
text: A Philadelphia redevelopment district has been flagged as a possible site for a large data center, exposing tensions among land reuse, power demand, and industrial strategy.

title: Se forma la tormenta tropical Dolly en el Atlántico
text: Tropical Storm Dolly has formed in the Atlantic and is expected to weaken before reaching the northeastern Caribbean, though rain impacts remain possible.

title: Japan killed 14,000 bears after a rise in deadly attacks on people – but is a cull the answer?
text: Japan’s mass bear cull after deadly attacks raises the question of whether lethal control can really address the structural drivers of human-wildlife conflict.

title: Planning for resilience
text:
The European Commission’s forthcoming Climate Resilience and Risk Management Integrated Framework should treat heatwaves not merely as emergency management, but as a single governance problem linking power-system resilience, adaptation finance, and regulatory coordination; otherwise member states will deepen vulnerability through fragmented responses and miss a window for institutionalization.

The argument is timed to Europe’s autumn 2026 legislative agenda, so the policy window is already open. It responds to the recent extreme summer and tries to turn seasonal crisis into the next round of institutional design.

This is an advance intervention in the EU’s adaptation and energy-security agenda as it moves toward legislative drafting and closure.

title: Why the clean energy transition needs information integrity
text:
The clean energy transition is now constrained not only by technology and cost, but by information manipulation that reshapes public perceptions, amplifies political resistance, and weakens policy enforceability; information integrity must therefore be treated as part of energy governance through platform rules, communication design, and regulatory oversight.

The piece is timed to a period when the transition is accelerating and renewables are breaking records, shifting the question from whether transition is possible to how it can be sustained in a contested information environment. It also speaks directly to current pressures on policy communication and narrative control.

This is a governance-toolbox intervention aimed at the intersection of platform governance and climate-policy coordination.

title: Climate change exposes 580 million children to 20 extra ‘heat-stress days’ every year
text:
The study turns unequal exposure of children to humid heat stress from an abstract vulnerability into a measurable inequality, showing that high exposure in South Asia, Southeast Asia, and West Africa reflects not just climate risk but the interaction of demography, historical emissions, and uneven adaptation resources; climate justice and public-health finance must therefore enter heat-risk governance together.

The findings are framed against the 2026 European heatwaves and current global heat-risk debates, stressing that this is not a future projection but an already visible distributional pattern. The study provides a new evidence baseline for adaptation, health, and equity debates now underway.

This is an evidence input for the heat-adaptation and child-health agenda, suitable for insertion into UNFCCC adaptation discussions and public-health finance talks.

title: Global climate adaptation governance: Why is it not legally binding?
source: Nina Hall, Åsa Persson · European Journal of International Relations
text:
The article explains why adaptation governance under the UN climate framework remains low in precision and obligation: adaptation is treated as a contested global public good and is often bundled with mitigation commitments, producing many rules but limited legalization. Its contribution is to recast adaptation governance not as absent but as present with weak constraint, and to show that this weakness is itself the product of political compromise.

The article examines the precision and obligation of adaptation-related decisions through analysis of primary UNFCCC documents, secondary literature, expert and negotiator interviews, and participant observation at climate negotiations.

Read alongside E3G’s "Planning for resilience": both ask how adaptation moves from ad hoc response into institutionalized governance.

Why does adaptation remain weakly legalized? adaptation governance legalization UNFCCC global public goods How do package deals shape adaptation commitments? mitigation adaptation bargaining international climate negotiations

title: Conceptualizing Climate Governance Beyond the International Regime
source: Chukwumerije Okereke, Harriet Bulkeley, Heike Schroeder · Global Environmental Politics
text:
The article argues that climate governance cannot be understood only through the lens of the international regime; subnational, private-sector, and cross-level actors must be included because climate policy is assembled through polycentric, multi-level governance. It emphasizes power, public-private authority relations, and the interaction of governing rationalities and practices.

The article uses conceptual review and theoretical synthesis, combining neo-Gramscian and governmentality perspectives to rebuild the analytical frame for climate governance.

Read alongside Inside Climate News’ "Will a Data Center Join the Philadelphia Bellwether District’s Mix of Manufacturers and Warehouses?": industrial redevelopment, data-center siting, and local energy governance all exemplify polycentric climate governance.

How does polycentric climate governance distribute power? polycentric governance climate governance public-private authority multi-level How does private authority enter climate policy? private authority governmentality climate policy global governance

title: Can Burnham justify giving the go ahead to oil drilling? Yes, but these must be the conditions | Michael Jacobs
text: The UK is due to revisit approvals for the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields after a court required new emissions assessments, shifting the dispute to whether conditional consent can coexist with net-zero commitments.

title: This is not a natural calamity: it is being done to us knowingly
text: The comment frames heat, wildfires, and marine heatwaves as a governance failure produced by human decisions, urging readers to treat climate harm as attributable rather than abstract tragedy.

title: Protecting our ‘most vital infrastructure’: Pushing back on desertification
text: UN News recasts land degradation as a failure of the infrastructure that underpins production, settlement, and resilience, rather than a background environmental issue.

title: The Trump Administration Has Spent Billions Boosting Gas Exports, Spurring More Fracking
text: The report argues that Trump-era fiscal and regulatory support for LNG exports is stimulating more fracking, converting an energy-security narrative into fossil-fuel expansion.

title: Burning Questions Confront Wildland Firefighters in Maine and Across New England
text: The warming wildfire season in New England is putting firefighting capacity, interstate resources, and federal policy pressure in the same frame.

title: The clean energy transition needs land. Can it help restore it too?
text: The report links land use by clean-energy infrastructure to land restoration, asking whether transition projects can also carry ecological repair obligations.

title: Trump Shuns E.V.s and Wind Power, But He’s Pouring Billions Into Batteries
text: The article notes that while the Trump administration shuns wind and EVs, it is heavily funding batteries for AI and defense needs while worrying about Chinese supply-chain dominance.

title: Trump’s Iran war supercharged EV sales everywhere except the U.S.
text: After the Iran conflict pushed up fuel prices, EV sales rose globally, but U.S. policy misalignment left the market advantage to Chinese automakers.

title: How climate finance can deliver in a multipolar world
text:
E3G argues that amid geopolitical fragmentation, high interest rates, and shrinking development assistance, climate finance must shift from simple capital mobilization to a package centered on multilateral development banks, debt instruments, and risk-sharing mechanisms, or developing countries will be priced out of the transition.

The piece responds to a moment when multilateral cooperation is weakening as fiscal space tightens. It moves climate finance from a general commitment to the operational question of delivery in a fragmented world.

It sits at the intersection of climate finance, debt sustainability, and development finance, with direct implications for MDB reform and pre-COP mobilization arrangements.

title: Q&A: What is ‘long-duration energy storage’ – and why does the UK need it?
text:
Carbon Brief frames long-duration energy storage as the infrastructure that allows the UK to move from hour-by-hour balancing toward day-to-week flexibility in a wind-and-solar system, while Ofgem’s cap-and-floor scheme turns underpriced system flexibility into a financeable asset that can lower system costs and reduce curtailment risk.

The Q&A comes just as Ofgem has identified 16 projects for potential support, showing that storage has moved from concept to regulatory selection. It shifts the discussion from technology primer to regulatory design and investment incentives.

It sits within UK electricity-market reform, system-flexibility allocation, and the investment framework for net-zero infrastructure.

title: Inter-organizational Relations and Policy Coordination
source: Adam Kamradt-Scott · Global Governance: A Review of Multilateralism and International Organizations
text:
The article focuses on policy coordination among international organizations and argues that, as member states face proliferating IOs, encouraging institutional collaboration has become a common governance response to reduce competition, conflict, and overlap. It also contends that ‘policy coordination’ remains underconceptualized in the literature and examines the Quadripartite’s efforts on antimicrobial resistance through national action plan adoption.

The article combines conceptual discussion with a case analysis of the Quadripartite’s coordination efforts, evaluating the diffusion of member states’ national action plans.

Read alongside E3G’s “How climate finance can deliver in a multipolar world” to see how multilateral coordination can be turned into workable financing and governance arrangements in a fragmented setting.

How does coordination become implementation? policy coordination international organizations implementation governance diffusion Which division of labor best reduces overlap? inter-organizational relations mandate overlap institutional collaboration multilateralism coordination

title: As Temperatures Get Hotter, Pesticides Are More Dangerous to Farmworkers
text: For the United States’ 2.4 million farmworkers, higher heat compounds pesticide exposure, heat stress, and the burden of protective clothing, turning occupational safety into a climate-labor overlap.

title: Offshore Wind Will Struggle Long After Trump’s Attacks
text: U.S. offshore wind is framed as facing not just a short-term political setback, but a long recovery even after the current window closes.

title: Judge Rejects Suit Against University of Michigan That Sought Emails on Climate Law
text: A lawsuit seeking emails from University of Michigan researchers on climate law was rejected, temporarily shielding the knowledge boundary around climate superfund legislation.

title: Extreme Heat Is The New Normal
text: Phoenix firefighters are keeping emergency services running with improvised cooling, showing how extreme heat is becoming a new baseline for public-service adaptation.

title: Hawaiian Islands brace for Lala this weekend
text: Lala could become the first hurricane on record to strike Hawaii’s Big Island, underscoring how extreme-weather risk is reaching places once seen as peripheral.

title: Utah group aims to make climate-friendly homes the norm
text: Utah Clean Energy is trying to make renewable-powered new homes the default, pushing decarbonization into building codes and the housing market’s front end.

title: Making nature investable through agrifood systems
text:
CPI argues that the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework sets macro-level goals for nature finance, but capital still cannot flow into agrifood systems because investors lack comparable, actionable signals for highly localized ecological outcomes; the result is a need for fit-for-purpose nature measurement tailored to geography, sector, and investment type to connect ecosystem integrity, supply-chain resilience, and the investment case.

The piece responds to the run-up to COP30, the spread of TNFD-aligned reporting, and the consolidation of MDB principles for nature finance. It pushes the agenda from disclosure toward investable outcomes, where the next contest is who defines measurable nature performance.

This sits at the technical-institutional interface where nature finance moves from frameworks and disclosure toward allocation standards, within the pre-COP30 mobilization agenda for natural capital.

title: Learning Hub Research Grantee Spotlight: I&P Ecosystems
text:
Using I&P Ecosystems’ research, CPI argues that small gender-climate funds in Sub-Saharan Africa struggle to scale not for lack of ambition, but because blended finance tools, concessional capital structures, and coordination mechanisms remain unstable, preventing catalytic capital from reliably reaching women entrepreneurs, smallholder farmers, and climate-affected communities.

The study is embedded in the urgent debate over Africa’s 2030 climate-resilience financing gap and the recent policy window in which gender and climate finance are being emphasized together. It shifts the question from whether more money is needed to how concessional capital should be structured and coordinated.

This is a methodological and allocation-rule problem in the catalytic-capital ecosystem, positioned at the intersection of regional funds, gender mainstreaming, and climate-finance instrument design.

title: Why land-use emissions have fallen by a third this century – in six charts
text:
Carbon Brief’s charts show that lower land-use emissions do not mean the governance task is finished; they indicate that policy and market pressure have begun to alter trajectories for deforestation, peatland loss, and forest degradation, raising the question of whether the decline is sufficient to support faster nature-climate co-governance or will be offset by rebound emissions elsewhere.

The piece uses century-scale data to revisit land-use emissions, responding to the question of how countries should interpret “progress” in the next round of NDCs, nature targets, and forest commitments. It also provides a time reference for whether the land sector can keep serving as a mitigation buffer before 2030.

This is an evidence interface between the NDC process and forest governance, sitting at the intersection of global nature targets and national mitigation commitments.

title: Orchestrating Global Climate Governance Through Data: The UNFCCC Secretariat and the Global Climate Action Platform
source: Laura Mai, Joshua Philipp Elsässer · Global Environmental Politics
text:
Using the Global Climate Action Portal as a case, the authors show how the UNFCCC Secretariat moved from using data to pressure state negotiations before Paris to using data to track and animate implementation after Paris, thereby reconfiguring nonstate commitments, data infrastructures, and governance authority. The article’s central claim is that data is not a neutral record-keeping tool but an organizing device in climate governance.

The article uses a single case study with process tracing around the Global Climate Action Portal, combined with conceptual analysis of changing data, infrastructure, and actor configurations.

Read this alongside this issue’s “Q&A: What does China’s 15th five-year plan for coal mean for climate action?” to compare how national planning and data-driven governance each shape climate action.

How does data shape implementation in climate governance? climate governance data infrastructure implementation tracking UNFCCC How is secretariat authority produced? international secretariat governance authority nonstate actors process tracing

title: The Show Must Go On? Revisiting the Script of International Climate Cooperation Ten Years After Paris
source: Florian Steig, Eva Lövbrand, Angela Oels, Jonathan Barnes, Diana Eriksson Lagerqvist, Marie Fischer, et al. · Global Environmental Politics
text:
Drawing on Foucault’s political thought and climate governmentality studies, this special issue examines how global climate governance seeks legitimacy ten years after Paris amid geopolitical rivalry, anti-climate populism, and accelerating crises. The introduction identifies four practices that stabilize the regime: promising future improvements, governmentalizing new frontiers, normalizing overshoot and climate disaster, and funneling climate expertise.

The introduction uses conceptual synthesis and normative-political analysis to map the regime’s power/knowledge mechanisms.

Read this alongside this issue’s “Offshore Wind Will Struggle Long After Trump’s Attacks” to see how anti-climate politics travels from domestic arenas into legitimacy pressures on governance.

How is legitimacy maintained in climate governance? climate legitimacy governmentality Paris Agreement political ecology How is overshoot normalized in policy discourse? overshoot climate discourse policy legitimation governance

title: ‘Waste colonialism’ – the Turkish city carrying the weight of Britain’s pollution problem
text: An investigation shows Britain exporting vast quantities of waste to poor districts in Adana, leaving farmers with microplastics, toxic smoke, and debris while shifting pollution costs abroad.

title: State of the Climate: A Dimming, Overheated Planet, With Degraded Oceans
text: The annual climate overview links record ocean heat, northern forests and tundra turning into net emitters, and accelerating ice loss from Greenland into one risk picture.

title: Pennsylvania Confronts an Unfamiliar Climate Hazard: Wildfire Smoke
text: Smoke drifting south from Canadian wildfires has pushed Pennsylvania child-care providers to treat air quality as a new everyday governance problem.

title: Watching the Atlantic: Could tropical waves exiting Africa make it past the wind shear?
text: The piece tracks whether tropical waves leaving Africa can survive wind shear, offering early signals on Atlantic cyclone formation.

title: ‘The Earth itself was screaming out:’ Bay Mills Indian Community fights pipeline permitting while enveloped in wildfire smoke
text: Amid wildfire smoke, the Bay Mills Indian Community is opposing a proposed 99-year extension for a pipeline permit, with the dispute centering on permitting and sovereignty.

title: New Amazon Data Center Stokes Worry It Would Be the Most Polluting Power Plant in the U.S.
text: Amazon’s investment in a gas-fired plant for a major Texas data center raises the question of whether AI-scale infrastructure is colliding with climate pledges.

title: Extreme Heat Comes for the Red Chile Capital of Pakistan
text: Pakistan’s red-chile growers are being forced to adapt as extreme heat and rising costs undermine long-standing cultivation practices.

title: Learning Hub Research Grantee Spotlight: MUBS Climate Finance and Sustainability Centre
text:
The Makerere University Business School Climate Finance and Sustainability Centre argues that without understanding local investors’ risk preferences, mandate constraints, and entry barriers in blended finance, climate capital will remain overly dependent on external deal design rather than building a durable domestic mobilization mechanism.

Uganda’s updated NDC has made the 2030 financing gap explicit, turning the question of who funds climate action and who absorbs structural risk into an immediate policy problem. The project also seeks to translate findings into reusable lessons for Africa.

This is upstream research within the broader agenda of domestic capital participation in blended finance structures, feeding into later investment design and policy engagement.

title: Factcheck: How nuclear, gas, wind and solar power are affected during heatwaves
text:
By comparing nuclear, gas, wind, and solar performance during heatwaves, Carbon Brief shows that power-system fragility does not come only from ‘intermittent’ renewables; warmer rivers, weaker cooling capacity, and demand spikes also constrain nuclear and gas supply, so resilience must be redesigned around technology-specific climate risks.

The 2026 European heatwaves have made supply constraints in France, Romania, Hungary, and Switzerland concrete, and the piece corrects power-planning assumptions under sustained warming. It also challenges narratives that reduce system stress to wind and solar alone.

It sits at the intersection of power reliability, climate adaptation, and energy transition, with direct agenda relevance for European electricity planning and heat-risk governance.

title: Eyes on Asia: shaping the global energy transition
text:
E3G argues that Asia is becoming the decisive arena for the global energy transition not merely because demand is growing fast, but because cooling needs, industrial expansion, and renewable deployment are rising together, forcing states to treat power systems, industrial policy, and financial mobilization within one transition frame.

The piece responds to a narrow but decisive window in which most new global energy demand over the next decade will come from Asia, making regional policy choices globally path-defining. It also warns against treating Asia merely as an implementation arena in climate diplomacy.

This is a strategic research input for framing Asia’s energy transition narrative and policy coordinates, linking to international energy cooperation and climate finance positioning.

title: Q&A: What is in China’s new five-year plan for climate change?
text:
Carbon Brief’s overview shows that China’s new five-year climate plan is tying targets, policy tools, and implementation more tightly together, implying that central planning is not mere signaling but a way to discipline local and sectoral action through coordination and institutionalized accountability.

The plan has just been released, making this the right moment to read China’s next round of climate governance instruments and implementation logic. It also offers clues for assessing China’s policy room in the next phase of international climate talks.

It sits at the start of China’s domestic climate policy cycle and will shape the credibility of subsequent external commitments and international negotiations.

title: Leveraging “Enabling Power” Through Awarding in Global Climate Governance: Catalytic Impacts of UNFCCC’s Global Climate Action Award
source: Aron Teunissen, Sander Chan · Global Environmental Politics
text:
Using the UNFCCC’s Global Climate Action Award, the authors examine how awarding mechanisms can amplify the replicability and diffusion of nonstate climate action through reputational incentives. But the extent of ‘catalytic impact’ depends on whether the mechanism addresses the key barriers actors face. The article shows that awards are not neutral recognition; they are mobilizing devices within global climate governance.

The article uses a conceptual framework and mechanism analysis centered on ‘enabling power’ to assess how awarding mechanisms shape catalytic impact.

Read it alongside this issue’s Carbon Brief signal on China’s new five-year climate plan: one piece asks how central planning disciplines implementation, the other how the UNFCCC uses awards to amplify action.

How do awards alter policy diffusion in climate governance? climate governance awards diffusion reputational incentives When do reputational incentives fail in transnational climate action? reputation transnational networks catalytic impact climate action

title: The Apocalyptic Climate Imaginary as Biopolitics: Avoid, Prepare, Endure (SI)
source: Diana Eriksson Lagerqvist, Johannes Stripple · Global Environmental Politics
text:
The article treats the apocalyptic climate imaginary as a biopolitical formation, arguing that collapse is not a one-off rupture but a chronic, uneven, and increasingly normalized governing condition. It distinguishes avoidance, preparation, and endurance as three orientations, showing that futures are actively redistributed through knowledge regimes, hierarchies of worth, and subject formation.

The article draws on Foucault and Lemke to conduct conceptual analysis and discourse interpretation.

Read it alongside Inside Climate News’s Pennsylvania wildfire-smoke story: smoke is not just an event, but something that normalizes ‘preparation’ and ‘endurance’ in everyday governance.

How does disaster imagination govern adaptation? biopolitics climate imaginary adaptation governance Who is expected to endure climate collapse? inequality subject formation resilience climate governance
